lead: Sensors and clocks give a microcontroller the state of the physical world: a voltage, a pulse width, or a serial frame. The CPU reads that number through an ADC pin or a bus. A real-time clock keeps calendar time when power fails. PWM works the other way: a timer pin switches a load on and off, and the load sees the average voltage. These blocks sit around the CPU in almost every embedded board: a temperature logger, a payment terminal with a clock, a fan controller.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.7 for the ADC step size, and Chapter 5.2 or Unit 4 timers for the PWM period.

blocks.text: A sensor turns a physical quantity into an electrical signal. The signal can be analog, a pulse width, a serial frame or a simple logic level. The CPU must know which type it is before it connects the sensor.

An LM35 gives 10 mV for every degree Celsius. Connect its output to one ADC channel, say channel 0. With an 8-bit ADC and Vref = 5 V, each code is 5/256 = 19.53 mV, as in Chapter 5.7. Temperature = sensor voltage ÷ 10 mV/°C. The LM35 needs no calibration in its normal range.

A light-dependent resistor (LDR) changes resistance with light. Put it in a divider with a fixed resistor; the junction voltage goes to an ADC. Bright light lowers LDR resistance, so the voltage moves one way. The direction depends on whether the LDR is the top or bottom resistor.
An infrared obstacle sensor has an IR LED and a photodiode. Its receiver gives a digital level: object present or absent. Connect it to a port pin, not an ADC.

The DHT11 sends temperature and humidity as a 40-bit frame on one wire: 8 bits humidity integer, 8 humidity decimal, 8 temperature integer, 8 temperature decimal, 8 checksum. The CPU times the start pulse and reads each bit from its high-time duration.
The HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor needs a 10 µs trigger pulse. Echo then stays high for the round-trip time of sound. Distance = echo width in µs ÷ 58, in centimetres.

The DS12887 is a real-time clock module with 128 bytes of battery-backed RAM. Fourteen of those bytes are clock, alarm and control registers; the rest are general RAM. It keeps seconds, minutes, hours, day, date, month and year.

The address and data pins are multiplexed on AD0-AD7. The CPU first puts an address on the bus and drops address strobe AS to latch it. It then asserts chip select CS and data strobe DS for the access, with RW choosing read or write. This is a multiplexed bus, not separate address and data pins.

Registers 00H to 09H hold seconds, seconds alarm, minutes, minutes alarm, hours, hours alarm, day of week, date, month and year. After reset they are in BCD. Register B has a binary-mode bit and a 12/24-hour bit. Register C holds interrupt flags. Register D has the valid-RAM bit; if it is 0, the backup battery is dead and the time is invalid.

Time can roll over during a read. Read seconds, minutes, hours, day, date, month and year; then read seconds again. If the second seconds value differs, repeat the whole block. This prevents mixing fields from two different seconds.
The DS1307 is a smaller RTC on I2C: two wires, SCL and SDA, same seconds-to-year idea in BCD.
PWM switches a load at a fixed period T and changes the on-time T<sub>on</sub>. The duty cycle sets the average. A 5 V rail at 25 percent gives 1.25 V; at 75 percent it gives 3.75 V.
D = T<sub>on</sub> / T, V<sub>avg</sub> = D × V<sub>cc</sub>
blocks.where: D is duty cycle; T<sub>on</sub> is on-time in seconds; T is period in seconds; V<sub>avg</sub> is average voltage in volts; V<sub>cc</sub> is supply voltage in volts.

blocks.text: A timer makes PWM with a counter and a compare value. The counter runs from 0 to the period count and reloads. When the count is below the compare value the pin is high; above it the pin is low. On the 8051, Timer 0 mode 2 gives auto-reload; an interrupt or compare logic sets the pin. On the MSP430, Timer_A compare channels drive the pin in hardware, so the CPU only writes the compare value.

Choose the frequency from the load. Too low: a lamp flickers and a motor jerks. Too high: switching loss and driver heating rise. Lamps often use a few hundred hertz to a few kilohertz. Small DC motors use 1 kHz to 20 kHz. A hobby servo expects 50 Hz and a 1 ms to 2 ms pulse; 1.5 ms is centre.
Uses: lamp dimming, DC motor speed, servo position, and LED brightness. The duty cycle sets the average; the period sets the switching frequency.

figure.caption: A 4 ms period from 250 Hz. The upper lane is on for 1 ms of every 4 ms, the lower lane for 3 ms; the average voltages are 1.25 V and 3.75 V.

spec.aria: Timing diagram of a 4 ms PWM period: the upper lane is on for 1 ms of every 4 ms, the lower lane for 3 ms, so the same period gives two different average voltages.

examples.question: An LM35 feeds ADC channel 0 of an 8-bit converter with V<sub>ref</sub> = 5 V. The code read is 0FH. Find the step size, the sensor voltage and the temperature. A 5 V rail drives a lamp through a transistor switched at 250 Hz with 25 percent duty cycle. Find the average voltage.
steps: Step 1: step size = V<sub>ref</sub>/2<sup>8</sup> = 5 V / 256 = 0.01953 V = 19.53 mV.
Step 2: 0FH = 15 decimal. Sensor voltage = 15 × 19.53 mV = 293 mV.
Step 4: period T = 1/f = 1/250 Hz = 0.004 s = 4 ms.
Step 5: on-time = D × T = 0.25 × 4 ms = 1 ms.
Step 6: average voltage = D × V<sub>cc</sub> = 0.25 × 5 V = 1.25 V.
examples.answer: The step size is 19.53 mV, the sensor voltage is 293 mV, the temperature is 29.3°C, and the lamp average voltage is 1.25 V.
examples.check:
step_mV = 5 / 256 * 1000
v_mV = 15 * step_mV
temp_C = v_mV / 10
period_ms = 1000 / 250
ton_ms = 0.25 * period_ms
avg_V = 0.25 * 5
print(round(step_mV, 2))
print(round(v_mV, 1))
print(round(temp_C, 1))
print(round(period_ms, 1))
print(round(ton_ms, 1))
print(round(avg_V, 2))

traps: The LM35 output is 10 mV/°C, not 10 V/°C. Convert 293 mV to 0.293 V before dividing by 0.01 V/°C; otherwise the answer is 1000 times too large.
RTC time registers are BCD until the binary bit in register B is set. Read 45H as 45 minutes, not as hexadecimal 69; a hex display gives nonsense.
The DS12887 has a multiplexed address/data bus. Latch the address with AS first; treating AD0-AD7 as separate address and data pins gives wrong register accesses.

Duty cycle is not frequency. Changing the compare value changes average voltage; changing the period count changes switching frequency. Same duty at two frequencies has the same average but different ripple.
HC-SR04 echo is a round trip. Divide the echo width in µs by 58 for centimetres, not by 29; the 10 µs trigger only starts the measurement.

quiz.q: What voltage does an LM35 produce at 30°C?
quiz.a: 300 mV, because it gives 10 mV per °C.

quiz.q: Why is a double read of the seconds register needed in the DS12887?
quiz.a: The clock can roll over during a multi-byte read; re-reading seconds and repeating if changed prevents mixing fields from two seconds.

quiz.q: An 8-bit ADC with V<sub>ref</sub> = 5 V reads code 0FH from an LM35. Find the temperature.
quiz.a: Step = 5/256 = 19.53 mV; voltage = 15 × 19.53 mV = 293 mV; temperature = 293 mV / 10 mV/°C = 29.3°C.

quiz.q: A 12 V rail is switched at 500 Hz with 40 percent duty cycle. Find the period, on-time and average voltage.
quiz.a: T = 1/500 Hz = 2 ms; T<sub>on</sub> = 0.40 × 2 ms = 0.8 ms; V<sub>avg</sub> = 0.40 × 12 V = 4.8 V.

quiz.q: A student reads DS12887 minutes as 45H after 39H and reports 69 minutes. Explain the error.
quiz.a: The register is in BCD; 45H means 45 minutes, not 4×16+5 = 69. Set the binary bit or convert BCD before arithmetic.

quiz.q: List the five bytes of a DHT11 frame.
quiz.a: Humidity integer, humidity decimal, temperature integer, temperature decimal, checksum.

quiz.q: Why is 50 Hz a poor PWM choice for an LED lamp but correct for a hobby servo?
quiz.a: 50 Hz gives a 20 ms period; an LED shows visible flicker and has poor dimming resolution. A hobby servo expects a 1 ms to 2 ms pulse every 20 ms.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial sensors often send 4–20 mA current loops or use I2C/SPI sensor hubs; safety systems add isolated front ends. RTCs in meters and payment terminals add temperature-compensated crystals and tamper detect. PWM is the base of switched-mode power supplies, LED drivers and field-oriented motor control. Search next for 'delta-sigma ADC', 'I2C sensor hub', 'DS3231 temperature-compensated RTC' and 'space vector PWM'.
